Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service Greenville-Spartanburg SC
1228 AM EST Tue Nov 24 2026

.WHAT HAS CHANGED...
Confidence remains high for a storm system to impact the region 
Wednesday into Thursday with the potential for locally heavy rain 
and gusty winds. Confidence in specific rainfall amounts remains 
low, however.

&&

.KEY MESSAGES...
1. A significant storm system could impact the area Wednesday
into Thursday bringing the potential for locally heavy rain and
frequent wind gusts.

&&

.DISCUSSION...
Key message 1: A significant storm system could impact the area 
Wednesday into Thursday bringing the potential for locally heavy 
rain and frequent wind gusts.

A rather complex forecast evolution is still on tap today through 
Thursday as a significant storm system evolves across the region. 
Ultimately, the track and strength of the system along with nearby 
synoptic features will dictate any impacts across the area. At a 
minimum, it will be a cold, rainy and windy period from Wednesday 
afternoon through at least Thursday morning. The upstream synoptic 
pattern is already taking shape as a tall western ridge extends from 
the Great Basin into British Columbia and Alberta. Downstream of the 
ridge, two pronounced pieces of energy are diving down the Front 
Range with the southern wave progged to dig over the Southern Plains 
while the northern wave develops into a closed upper low over the 
Northern Plains into the Midwest. At the surface, high pressure will 
have shifted across the Great Lakes and into New England and will 
instigate the development of a strong and classic Cold Air Damming 
(CAD) wedge by Wednesday morning. The overall gist of the forecast 
thereafter remains relatively unchanged with all guidance depicting 
surface cyclogenesis along the Atlantic coast of Florida while a 
secondary and weaker low develops along a coastal baroclinic zone 
draped along the Gulf Coast. The southern upper trough takes on a 
negative tilt as it lifts across the southeast and helps to rapidly 
deepen a coastal cyclone. Low-level mass response will foster the 
formation of a highly anomalous 60-70kt easterly low-level jet that 
will translate across the area Wednesday night. Increasing 
isentropic ascent atop the CAD wedge will allow for precipitation to 
blossom from southeast to northwest by Wednesday afternoon and will 
help to further lock in the CAD via diabatic processes. The result 
being chilly temperatures with highs struggling to climb out of the 
40s.

As for potential impacts, there's still some degree of uncertainty 
as the forecast hinges on multiple complex moving pieces that will 
dictate the finer details. This is most apparent in ensemble 
sensitivity analysis which specifically keys in on the timing, 
strength and tilt of the upper troughs along with the strength and 
amplitude of a downstream ridge extending from offshore into New 
England. Cluster analysis paints two main scenarios with a more 
impactful solution being driven by a stronger and favorably located 
closed low over the Ohio Valley that acts to draw the surface low 
farther inland. The other scenario is a less favorable interaction 
with the Ohio Valley closed low which would keep the surface low 
farther east and generally along the coast. Regardless, at a 
minimum, several inches of rain appears likely, which wouldn't pose 
a major concern for hydro issues. However, should the low get pulled 
farther inland a band of locally heavy rain could set up more into 
the area with additional support from a band of intense mid-level 
frontogenesis on the northwest flank of the low. Any focused locally 
heavy rain could yield some degree of hydro issues should rainfall 
rates tick up into the 3"/hr range. Winds will also be gusty as the 
surface pressure gradient tightens between the parent surface high 
fueling the CAD wedge and the coastal surface low. This will at 
least result in 30-40mph gusts with the potential for isolated power 
outages. A farther inland low track with a tighter pressure gradient 
could result in a higher end scenario with wind gusts of 40-50mph.

The coastal storm lifts north through the day Thursday with the 
associated precipitation shield also gradually lifting out of the 
area. Most rain should move out of the area by late afternoon on 
Thursday. A brief period of northwest flow showers and perhaps snow 
showers could occur across the mountains late Thursday through 
Friday, but confidence is rather low right now as to how much 
moisture would wrap around before forcing lifts out of the area. 
Thereafter, quiet weather returns through much of the weekend.

&&

.AVIATION /06Z TUESDAY THROUGH SATURDAY/...
At KCLT and elsewhere: Dry and VFR through the 06Z TAF period. 
Clouds will increase through daybreak becoming BKN to OVC. The South 
Carolina Upstate terminals will remain BKN to OVC much of the TAF 
period but the western North Carolina terminals should see cloud 
cover decrease throughout the day, eventually becoming FEW (possibly 
even SKC). Cloud cover will increases again late tonight into 
daybreak Wednesday across the western North Carolina terminals 
becoming SCT to BKN. Winds east of the mountains will be NE through 
the period, with low-end gusts developing later this morning (with 
the exception of KHKY). Winds at KAVL will be NW through at least 
mid-morning before turning more E this afternoon and eventually S/SE 
this evening. Low-end gusts should linger through at least daybreak 
at KAVL. Should see a brief lull in gust activity across the South 
Carolina Upstate terminals late this afternoon into early this 
evening so went with a TEMPO to account for lighter speeds from 22Z-
01Z. KCLT should see a longer break in gusts from early evening to 
late tonight before returning early Wednesday morning. 

Outlook: Widespread rain, gusty winds and associated restrictions 
develop Wednesday into Thursday as a strong low pressure system 
tracks across the terminals. Drier and VFR conditions return 
Thursday night into Friday but gusty winds will continue.
